lesson.title: Grabbing a Chunk: Introduction to String Slicing
lesson.summary: Slicing extracts a whole substring from a string by specifying a start and stop index separated by a colon, producing a brand new string rather than modifying the original.
lesson.body:
Indexing retrieves exactly one character at a time, but plenty of real tasks need a whole chunk: the area code from a phone number, the file extension from a filename, the first three letters of a word. Slicing generalizes indexing to handle exactly this. The syntax word[start:stop] returns a new string containing the characters from index start up to, but not including, index stop. That 'up to but not including' rule, often called a half-open range, is easy to state and slightly tricky to internalize, but it is consistent everywhere Python uses ranges, including the range() function used in loops.

Take "PYTHON" again and slice out characters 1 through 3:

word = "PYTHON"
print(word[1:4])

Remember the index map from before: index 1 is Y, index 2 is T, index 3 is H, and index 4 is O. The slice word[1:4] collects indices 1, 2, and 3, which is exactly three characters, Y, T, and H, stopping right before reaching index 4. The result is the new string "YTH", and O at index 4 is deliberately excluded. Counting the length of the slice is a useful sanity check: stop minus start, or 4 minus 1, equals 3, matching the three characters returned.

Either boundary of a slice can be left out, and Python fills in a sensible default. Omitting start defaults to the very beginning of the string, index 0, and omitting stop defaults to the very end. So word[:3] returns "PYT", the first three characters, and word[3:] returns "HON", everything from index 3 to the end. Leaving out both, word[:], returns a full copy of the string, every character included. These shortcuts come up constantly in real code because they read naturally: word[:3] reads as 'the first three characters' and word[3:] reads as 'everything after the first three.'

A slice never raises an IndexError, even when its boundaries reach past the edges of the string, which is a genuine and useful difference from plain indexing. word[1:100] on a six-character string simply returns everything from index 1 to the end, "YTHON", instead of crashing, because Python quietly clamps an out-of-range stop value down to the string's actual length. This forgiving behavior makes slicing safer than indexing when the exact length of a string is uncertain, though it also means a slicing mistake can silently return less data than intended rather than announcing itself with an error, so it is still worth checking your boundaries carefully.

Every slice produces a completely new string; the original string referenced by word is untouched by word[1:4], which matters once string immutability is covered in more depth, and it also means the result of a slice can be stored in its own variable, printed directly, or fed straight into another string operation just like any other string value. Slicing also builds directly on the indexing you already know, since word[i] for a single index and word[start:stop] for a range both use the same square-bracket notation and the same zero-based counting, just applied to one position versus a whole span of them.
